en: The Brahmajāla-sūtra: The Questions of the Brahmin Aṭṭhaka, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time...
There were five hundred bhikṣus present.

In the city of Śrāvastī, there were five hundred brāhmaṇas who, accompanied by their followers, went out from the city together to their own rural dwellings. There they sat down together and held a discussion, saying:

"When human beings first arose upon the earth, we brāhmaṇas were the first caste; the second caste was the kṣatriya, the third was the vaiśya, and the fourth was the śūdra. Our caste is the most honorable."

"When we first arose upon the earth as human beings, all were of our lineage; when first born, they issued from the mouth. Now, people of the present age conversely emerge from below. Among those who dwell under heaven, our lineage is the most honored."

"Our lineage consists entirely of the descendants of the seventh son of Brahmā; yet the Buddha conversely claims that all under heaven belong to but a single kind. The Buddha treats our lineage as equal to the Kṣatriyas, the farmers, and the artisans."
"Our ancestors all ascended to the Brahma Heaven; yet the Buddha treats our lineage as equal to that of ordinary people.
They deliberated among themselves, "Who can debate with the Buddha and distinguish this matter of our lineage?"

At that time, there was a brahmin who had a son aged fifteen or sixteen, named Āṭavaka Mahāmuni. He was proficient in the arts of writing and knew the affairs of both past and future; among five hundred brahmins, there was none who could equal him, and all served him as their teacher. He was able to expound the sūtras and understood the matters of the world.
The great sage Āṭavaka possessed extraordinary physical marks, and the brahmins deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Only Āṭavaka is able to converse with the Buddha; none of us can converse with him."
The five hundred men together addressed Āṭavaka, saying:

"The Buddha regards all people under heaven as a single caste, whereas our own caste is distinct from that of the Kṣatriyas, the Vaiśyas, and the Śūdras. Our lineage descended from the Brahmā Heaven; we were born from his mouth, while the people of the present world are born, on the contrary, from below."
The Buddha said,
"There are four kinds of people in the world, and all four are excellent.
He wished that Āṭavaka would deign to go together with him to engage in discussion with the Buddha.

Aṭṭhaka said: "The Buddha upholds the true path and is able to respond to those who uphold the true path; yet, though you wish to maintain the Brahmin lineage, you do not possess the path or the correctness of the path."
The five hundred men all said, "We take Āṭavaka as our teacher; why do we not go to him to discuss these four matters?
This was repeated a second and a third time, whereupon Āṭavaka rose and went with the five hundred men to the Buddha at the Jeta Grove.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"There is a son of a brāhmaṇa named Aṭṭhaka, fifteen or sixteen years of age, who has come with five hundred elderly brāhmaṇas and is standing outside."
The Buddha said,
"Call him in. Ānanda went out and invited Āḷāra Kālāma to enter.
The five hundred people, including Aṅgiras, all remained standing; they did not prostrate before the Buddha, but said of themselves, "We have a minor matter we wish to ask the Buddha."
The Buddha said,
"You may sit.
Aṭṭhaka Āḷavaka addressed the Buddha:
"I wish to ask a question; would you be willing to answer it?
The Buddha said, "If you have any doubts, speak them."

Ampāyana said: "Our caste practices the Way differently from those of the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; we say that our caste is the lineage of the sons of Brahmā, and when our ancestors were first born, they all emerged from [his] mouth, and upon death, they all ascended to heaven."
The Buddha replied:
"In my sutras, I do not teach that there are different castes.
If a brāhmaṇa marries a kṣatriya woman, the kṣatriya woman gives birth to a son; [and so on]."
A kṣatriya marries a woman from a farming family, and she bears him a son;
a farmer marries a woman from an artisan family, and she bears him a son;
an artisan marries a woman from a brahmin family, and she bears him a son.
The Buddha said:

"In my sutras, the practice of giving is fundamental. Those who practice the goodness of giving are the greatest of seeds; those who are honored and noble in the world all attain such status through the practice of giving, not by means of their lineage."

In incalculable kalpas of my past lives, I was also the son of a brahmin, the son of a kṣatriya, the son of a farmer, and the son of a craftsman; I have attained the status of a prince myself, and now I am a Buddha.
The Buddha said to Āṭavaka:
“I shall ask you one thing; answer it as it truly is.
The Buddha spoke thus:
“If one sees a son of a virtuous family in this world who has become a slave to another, can that slave, in turn, be released from slavery and become a son [to his master]?
Āṭavaka addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have heard that such a thing occurs in the country of the Yuezhi.”
The Buddha asked, "For what reason? [He replied:

"A son of good family becomes a slave, and a slave conversely becomes a son to someone else. This is because the slave’s intention and conduct were virtuous, so he was made a son; whereas the son who became a slave did so because his intention and conduct were evil, and he merely sold himself to become a slave to another."
“If you say that people have such a nature, in what place does this human nature reside?
The Buddha said:

“Suppose there are these four castes—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—who take great pleasure in killing, take great pleasure in stealing, take great pleasure in sexual misconduct, take great pleasure in double-tongued speech, take great pleasure in harsh speech, take great pleasure in lying, take great pleasure in slandering others, take pleasure in associating with fools, take pleasure in anger, and take pleasure in performing sacrifices.”
"If one acts in this way, would they not fall into hell?

Āṛṣṭiṣeṇa replied, "According to the teachings of the Brahmin caste, although such evils exist, our lineage is the most honored. We are the descendants of Brahmā’s son; we were born from his mouth, and upon death, we shall all ascend to heaven."
The Buddha said:

"If there are those of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes who have no intent to kill, no intent to steal, no intent to commit sexual misconduct, no intent for double-tongued speech, no intent for harsh speech, no intent for false speech, no delight in slandering others, no delight in following delusion, and no delight in anger or sacrificial rites—would such people not be reborn in the heavens when they die?"
Āṭavaka said, “In this way,
they are all born in the heavens.
The Buddha said:
“If you ask where these categories reside,” the Buddha said,
“all human categories arise from mind, thought, and consciousness.”
Those whose mind, intellect, and consciousness practice virtue will be born among the heavens and humans;
those whose mind, intellect, and consciousness are evil will enter the realms of insects, beasts, ghosts, spirits, and hell.
If there are those among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras who practice evil, they all enter together into the three evil realms.
In such a case, where would their lineage reside?

The practices of the Brahmin caste may be either good or evil; the practices of the Kṣatriya caste may also be either good or evil; the practices of the Vaiśya caste may also be either good or evil; and the practices of the Śūdra caste may also be either good or evil.
If you yourselves claim that there is a seed, where does such a seed reside?

Whether a Brahmin harbors malice toward this space, or a Kṣatriya, a farmer, or a craftsman harbors malice toward this space, it cannot be injured or harmed; their mental intentions are equal, yet the Brahmin merely harbors a mind of self-exaltation toward the world.

Suppose there were people of the Brahmin caste, the Kṣatriya caste, the Vaiśya (farmer) caste, and the Śūdra (artisan) caste who entered the waters of a large river and each bathed themselves, causing their dirt to fall into the water. Would it be possible to distinguish and know, "This is the dirt of a Brahmin, this is the dirt of a Kṣatriya, this is the dirt of a Vaiśya, and this is the dirt of a Śūdra"?
Ampāyana said: "If impurities exist within the waters of a great river, one should know where they reside. [The Buddha replied:

"If you do not even know where the impurities of humans reside, yet you instead claim that my lineage dwells in the heavens, originating from the mouth, while other people originate from below, and that my lineage is the most noble among men."
The Buddha said to Āṭavaka:

“Suppose a king hears that in a certain kingdom, district, county, or village there is a brāhmaṇa and his son who are highly accomplished, a kṣatriya and his son who are highly accomplished, a farmer and his son who are highly accomplished, or a craftsman and his son who are highly accomplished; the king then summons them all to serve as his ministers. Does the king inquire after their caste?”
As for those of high talent and clear understanding, the King first grants them fine commanderies and kingdoms.
Why does the King not inquire about your lineage?
If you claim to have a lineage, you are merely Āṛṣakas!
If the precepts were present [in you],
why did those five hundred elders— who sat above you— fail to reprove you for your conduct or for acting as their teacher?

Whether there be Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those of other castes, when they are all together by a great fire in the cold season, the heat of the fire does not reach only one kind; the warmth is equal for all alike.

If there is a large boat crossing a river, and members of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes are all together on one boat, the boat does not ferry across the Brahmin caste alone, nor does it ferry across the other castes alone.
The Buddha asked Āṭavika:

"If the seeds of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes are likewise placed within a mother's womb for the same duration of ten months, is there any increase or decrease [in their development]?"
Aṭṭhaka said: "It is exactly ten months, with neither increase nor decrease. [The Buddha asked:
"Why do you all claim that you are the descendants of the sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth?"
The Brahmin caste, the Kṣatriya caste, the Vaiśya caste, the Śūdra caste, and other castes as well—why do the sun and moon not shine exclusively upon you alone?
"Why do you claim to illuminate other lineages as well? Āṭavaka replied,
"My own lineage proclaims itself superior to all other lineages."
The Buddha said to Āṭavika:
"If there is a donkey father and a horse mother, and a horse gives birth to a foal, what is that offspring called? Āṭavika replied:
"It is called a mule.
Its father was not named 'mule,' nor was its mother named 'mule.
Why, then, is it named 'mule'?"
“I called my ancestors ‘mules,’ so I followed their word and called them mules.
“If there is a horse father and a donkey mother, and the donkey gives birth to a son, what name should that offspring be called? It is a hinny.”
"The father did not name him 'Gongxu,' nor did the mother name him 'Gongxu. How then do we know he is a *gongxu*?
[The other replied: "My ancestors called him *gongxu*, and so I follow their words and call him *gongxu*."
“If a Brahmin marries a Kṣatriya woman and a son is born to that Kṣatriya woman, what should he be named?
Should he be called one of the Brahmin caste?”
"Are you of the Kṣatriya caste? Āṭavaka replied,
"I do not know what caste I should call myself."
The Buddha said:
"If you do not recognize your own kind, how can you be called mules or hinny?

When a Kṣatriya woman bears a son to a Brāhmaṇa, she enters your gates, follows your sacrificial rites, and follows your lineage; yet this child subsequently becomes noble and wise. Should you serve him, or should you cast him out?"
"How should we serve him?

A Brahmin marries a woman from a farming family, and that woman bears him a son. That son possesses a mind for killing, a mind for stealing, a mind for sexual misconduct, a mind for double-tongued speech, a mind for harsh speech, a mind for lying, a mind for slandering, a mind that delights in following folly, a mind of malice, and a mind for ritual sacrifice. If there is one who acts in such ways, would you follow along with him?"
“We will not associate with you.
Since your mind, consciousness, and intentions have performed evil deeds, we shall expel you and not admit you among our ranks.”
The Buddha said:
"You claim yourselves to be descendants of the Son of Brahmā, born from his mouth and destined to ascend to heaven upon death.
Yet you merely see the mind, consciousness, and intellect performing evil deeds and immediately pursue one another; why do you discourse on such lineages?"
The Buddha said:

"If there are those of the Brahmin caste who are unfilial toward their parents, who delight in killing and stealing, and who commit the ten unwholesome deeds, to which realm will they go when they die?"
Aṅgīrasa said: "One whose mind, consciousness, and mental formations act in such a manner shall, upon death, enter hell.
The Buddha said:
"You fellows say, 'Our lineage is originally from Brahmā; we were born from his mouth and are the most honored among men.
Why then have we entered into hell?
The Buddha said:"
"Among the people of the world, there are no distinct species, nor is there anyone who is eternally superior or sublime.
It is when one's mind and will are good and one's conduct is virtuous that one is noble;
it is when the mind and conduct are evil that one is base."
Aṭṭhaka the Ābhassara reflected to himself:
"I did not originally wish to come; it was the people who together compelled me to come.
He pondered thus:
"I originally intended not to dispute with the Buddha, yet I continued to say that the Buddha's Way is correct.
The Buddha said,
"If at first you had said that people should plant what is excellent, you would now instead come to me and say that my mind and will are excellent."
Āḷāra Kālāma thought to himself,
"The Buddha’s words have blocked my way both before and behind.
Then the Buddha said to Āḷāra Kālāma:
“In the distant past, there were seven brahmins, all of whom possessed the Way and performed daily sacrifices to the heavens.
These seven brahmins also proclaimed their own doctrine, saying:

‘We are the descendants of the Son of Brahmā; we were born from his mouth, whereas ordinary people are born from below. Our lineage differs from that of ordinary people; when those of our lineage die, they shall all ascend to heaven.’”
The Buddha said:
"At that time, I was also a practitioner of the Way, named Ākhyāta; the multitude collectively called my path the 'Path of Heaven.
At that time, I saw seven brahmins at a fire-altar sacrifice, and all those brahmins said:"
"We shall die in this manner; the fire-light shall ascend to heaven.
The Buddha said:

"I saw what you were doing, so I transformed my body. Holding a banner with a golden handle in my hand and wearing white robes, I borrowed a carriage from a man and went to the place where the seven brāhmaṇas were."
At that time, seven brahmins were walking up and down; when they and their followers saw me, they called out to me, saying: "Brahmin!
From where have you come along this path?"
The seven brahmins said:
"If this is the Way of Heaven, it is roughly equal to ours; why then do you wear fine robes, ride in a carriage, and hold a golden banner in your hand?"
From what place did you arise?
Where do you wish to go?
From where have you come?
"Why have you come here?
At that time, I did not speak to them.
Seeing that I did not answer, they all became angry; having cast spells upon me, they sought to cause my death.
"The more you recite incantations over me, the more beautiful my face becomes;
the more you continue to recite them, the more radiant my complexion grows.
At this, the seven brāhmaṇas were greatly astonished and said:
"What we have cursed always dies;
now that I have cursed him, why has his facial complexion become even better?
He called out "A-xi" once more.
He thought to himself:
"In what kind of path do you wish to proceed?
Āṭavika immediately replied:
"My way and intention are superior; why are you all angry?
Have you not heard of the Way of Heaven taught by Master Axi? They replied:
"I did not hear it.
"Worthy practitioner!
When we meet, we should inquire after one another; why do you become angry with me?"
Āṭavika said: "I have heard what you say:
that the brahmins of the world are the descendants of the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth, and uniquely honored among men."
For this reason, I have come to ask you:
"If you kindle this fire to sacrifice to the gods, according to what dharma and by following which teacher’s path do you perform this sacrifice?
You no longer hear of it from your ancestors."
The seven brāhmaṇas said:
"Our ancestors served as our models.
The ascetic Ātreya said:
"Was your great-grandmother a Brahmin woman or the daughter of another?
They replied,
'We do not know whether our great-grandmother was a Kṣatriya woman, a woman from a farming family, or a woman from a craftsman's family.'"

"I do not know whether my great-grandmother was born of a Brahmin, nor whether you love another person who gives birth to one of your own kind. If you do not even know your own ancestors, how can you know that your ancestors descended from Brahmā to be born here?"
"Is the heart of a woman untrustworthy?
If you all knew about people in the world, how do husbands and wives unite to produce children?
They all replied, "We do not know."
"If you do not know my ancestors, nor do you know the person from whom I was born, why do you direct your anger toward me?

When ordinary people meet one another, they should first exchange greetings regarding their respective status; only after understanding a person's intent may one then become angry. Why, then, do you become angry first?"
Do you know when the child first enters the womb?
When the father possesses lustful tendencies and the mother harbors a heart of longing, that which is to become the child is formed through the union of these three factors.
Regarding what it means to be a son: who causes one to be warm-hearted toward one's parents so as to become a true son?

While the child is in the womb, perhaps due to evil deeds committed in a previous life, they may be blind, deaf, mute, hunchbacked, lame, or crippled; yet the parents remain unaware of these conditions.

When parents are close to giving birth and carry their child in the womb, they cannot yet know whether that child will be handsome or ugly; how then can you all know that your ancestors were descendants of the Son of Heaven of Brahmā, born from his mouth, and uniquely honored among men?
The Buddha told Āṭavaka:
"In a previous age, even seven brahmins were able to kill people through incantations; at that time, I did not permit your kind, nor did I take what you said into account."

"Now that I have become a Buddha, if you were to come and speak thus again, saying, 'I am a descendant of the sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, the sole honored one among men,' I would say this to you, Āṭavaka:
'Reflect upon my words; when children are born in the world, those who nourish them are their parents, and those who bring them to maturity are their teachers.'"
The Brahmin Aṭṭhaka, together with five hundred Brahmins and other Brahmins, reflected:
"In the past, I served as the teacher for seven Brahmins; those seven Brahmins were all men of great virtue who could kill people through incantations.
Now, I shall distinguish and explain the Path."
"This person has seeds that become one hundred from one, one hundred becomes one thousand, one thousand becomes ten thousand, and ten thousand becomes one.
Āṭavaka and the other brahmins all stepped forward and touched their heads to the Buddha’s feet, saying:
"We do not understand how one becomes one hundred, one hundred becomes one thousand, one thousand becomes ten thousand, and ten thousand becomes one."
"What does this mean?
The Buddha said:

"In this world, there are many people who greedily delight in birth and death. One person produces sons and grandsons, and these subsequently divide into a hundred households; yet, all those hundred households seek the Way as one and the same Way."
What is the single path? It is the unconditioned path (*asaṃskṛta-mārga*).
In this way, one becomes a thousand, and a thousand becomes ten thousand.
Āṭavaka knelt down before him and said:
"May you deign to have compassion for us as you do for the śramaṇas; let there be no heart of resentment, but please accept our invitation to come and gather together with us."
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
You all have not eaten since this morning.
They all rose, placed their heads at the Buddha's feet in prostration, and departed.
The Sūtra on the Brahmin Aṭṭhaka’s Questions to the Honored One of the Śākyas.
